analysis.one_liner: Bans new offshore oil and gas drilling and ocean waste dumping off California's coast.
analysis.headline: The bill to protect California's coastal waters from new offshore drilling never got a committee vote before Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have designated the waters extending 200 miles off the California coast as the California Ocean Sanctuary. Within that area, no federal agency could issue new leases or permits for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, and no existing lease could be renewed once it lapsed. It also banned ocean incineration and harmful dumping, and barred ships from carrying waste through the sanctuary en route to disposal sites. It explicitly left commercial and recreational fishing untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live along, visit, or make their living from the California coast: beachgoers and tourists, coastal businesses, and commercial and recreational fishermen. The bill's stated purpose was to shield the coastline from oil spills and drilling infrastructure and to strengthen fisheries by keeping drilling and waste disposal out of the sanctuary.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any federal agency from issuing new leases, permits, or licenses for oil, gas, or mineral exploration or extraction anywhere in the 200-mile sanctuary off California [S3].

Bans ocean incineration and harmful ocean dumping within the sanctuary, including permits for onshore facilities that would feed waste into it, and bars vessels from carrying waste through the sanctuary on the way to disposal [S3].
Leaves commercial and recreational fishing entirely unregulated, so fishermen keep full access while the waters they fish are protected from drilling and dumping [S3].
Cites the threat of fossil fuel development and toxic waste burning and dumping as risks of 'irreparable damage' to a coastal resource with recreational, economic, and ecological value [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding or seeking offshore leases off California, and firms in the ocean incineration and hazardous waste disposal business, which would lose access to new sites and future customers in the sanctuary.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets existing oil and gas leases continue to operate until they lapse, so drilling already underway would not stop immediately — the ban applies only to new activity and to leases after they expire or are terminated [S3].

The strongest good-faith objection is that locking up a 200-mile zone of the Outer Continental Shelf forecloses domestic energy production and could raise costs, a tradeoff the bill accepts without compensation or phase-in [S3].
Banning ocean incineration and dumping routes without creating alternatives could push waste disposal toward other sites or methods, including onshore options with their own costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the California coast, the benefits — protected fisheries, beaches, and coastline free of new drilling rigs and waste traffic — are broad and long-lasting, while the costs fall on a small set of energy and waste-disposal firms. The main honest caveat is the bill's grandfathering: active leases keep producing until they run out, so protection arrives slowly. The main honest objection is the energy-supply tradeoff of permanently closing a large offshore area.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the first day of the new Congress, sent jointly to two House committees, farmed out to three subcommittees, and never came back out — no markup, no floor vote, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representatives Barbara Boxer and Mel Levine of California introduced the bill on January 3, 1989, the first day of the 101st Congress [S3][S5].

It was referred jointly to the House Committees on Interior and Insular Affairs and Merchant Marine and Fisheries, then split among three subcommittees covering water and offshore energy, fisheries and wildlife, and oceanography [S5].
The committees requested executive comment from the Interior, Commerce, Energy, and EPA — a routine early step — but no action followed [S5].
No committee or subcommittee vote is recorded, and the bill never reached the House floor; it expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas interests and ocean waste-disposal firms kept the status quo: existing leasing and permitting rules stayed in place, and the 200-mile sanctuary was never created. California's coastal waters remained open to future federal leasing decisions.

for.name: Rep. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill establishing the California Ocean Sanctuary and its drilling and dumping bans.

for.name: Rep. Mel Levine
for.what_they_did: Joined Boxer in introducing the bill on the first day of the Congress.

for.name: 34 of 257 House Democrats and 2 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors (36 total), giving the bill a small bipartisan group of backers.

against.name: House Committees on Interior and Insular Affairs and Merchant Marine and Fisheries
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its day-one referral, split it among three subcommittees, and never reported it out for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Offshore oil and gas industry
against.role: Would-be lessees off the California coast
against.what_they_did: The bill's leasing and exploration bans were aimed squarely at offshore oil and gas development, the industry whose access the measure would have ended within the sanctuary.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 36 cosponsors included 34 Democrats and 2 Republicans, so early support crossed party lines, though no votes were ever recorded to test the split.

industries.note: The bill bars new federal leases and permits for oil, gas, and mineral extraction across a 200-mile zone off California, and lets existing leases lapse out of existence. Its cost is the industry's lost access; its benefit is coastal protection for the public.

industries.industry: Ocean incineration and hazardous waste disposal firms
industries.note: The bill prohibits ocean incineration and harmful dumping in the sanctuary, blocks permits for onshore facilities feeding waste into it, and bans waste-carrying vessels from transiting the area. The public's gain from cleaner waters is these firms' lost disposal options.

The bill leaves fishing entirely unregulated while the bill's findings tie sanctuary protection to enhanced fisheries, so fishermen keep access and the waters they fish are shielded from drilling and dumping.
The bill protects beaches and coastal waters from new drilling infrastructure and waste traffic, which its findings describe as essential to the coast's recreational and economic value.
